newsitem.title: CHINA: China to lift fund freeze to expand stock market.
newsitem.headline: China to lift fund freeze to expand stock market.

text.p: China will lift a three-year ban on the listing of mutual funds for securities investment by the end of this year with the aim of injecting liquidity into its fast-expanding stock markets, analysts said on Friday.

New rules governing trading of the funds will shortly be promulgated, ending a ban on the listing of mutual funds on the national stock markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen in effect since 1993, official media have reported.
"The adoption of the new regulations will be a signal that the freeze over the funds market will thaw," official Xinhua news agency quoted a magazine run by the State Planning Commission as saying.
"The thaw is aimed at giving a boost to the stock markets," said a senior stock analyst with a Chinese securities house.

"The stock markets have never expanded faster than they are doing this year since they were set up six years ago," he added. "The central government wants the markets to boom and they have opened this key channel for liquidity."
In the early 1990s, Beijing encouraged the set-up of mutual funds which raised money from individuals to invest largely in stocks.
Around 70 such funds were established with an official promise that they would be listed like shares on the national markets, attracting many investors who saw an opportunity for quick profits.

But after the listing of about 22 funds on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges, it emerged that many were poorly managed and were losing money, which prompted the authorities to ban new listings in 1993.
There are still about 50 such funds, mostly run by securities houses and brokerages, which have not been listed. Most are closed funds from which investors cannot retrieve their funds for 10 years.

The failure of China's first effort at mutual funds has resulted in poor liquidity composition for China's stock markets with speculative funds dominating and stable stock investment funds comprising less than one percent, stock analsts said.
"This is one of the reasons why China's stock markets are dominated by speculators and are in bad need of long-term investors," said a fund manager with Shenyin & Wanguo Securities.

In the past few months, Beijing has said it would allow the stock markets to play a bigger role and analysts said the central government was aiming to make the markets more competitive in the run-up to the Hong Kong takeover in mid-1997.
With official blessing, Shanghai has listed 79 new domestic A share firms so far this year compared with 69 for the whole of the former peak year of 1994, and Shenzhen 59 against 40.
Official media reports said the new fund rules would encourage more institutional investors and boost the stock markets.
The rules will include provisions that each fund must raise at lease one million yuan ($120,500) before it can apply for a listing, according to the media reports.
They must invest no less than 20 percent of their capital in treasury bonds and with a minimum of 60 percent in stocks and bonds, the rules said. ($1 = 8.3 yuan)
